content.text:
We are getting duplicate invoice emails again. Support forwarded two customers this morning who each got the same invoice PDF roughly four minutes apart, and last week a customer received nine. It is not every invoice — maybe one in three hundred — but the ones that duplicate are embarrassing and the support load is real.

The relevant code is ```internal/queue/dispatcher.go``` and ```internal/queue/consumer.go```. Each worker goroutine pulls invoice IDs off a Redis list called ```billing:pending``` and calls ```store.MarkEmailed(ctx, id)``` when it is done. The duplicates are all "email sent" jobs, never "generate PDF" jobs, if that narrows anything for you.
Reproduce it first. I do not want a fix written against a theory. Can you run the consumer under the race detector and get me the actual report?

Good instinct, and it turned out to be two separate things, so I ran both.

```go test -race -count=200 -run TestConsumerConcurrent ./internal/queue/...``` took four minutes and produced this about once every thirty runs:

```
WARNING: DATA RACE
Write at 0x00c0001b4010 by goroutine 447:
  billing.store.(*pgStore).MarkEmailed()
      internal/store/invoice.go:212
Previous read at 0x00c0001b4010 by goroutine 512:
  billing.store.(*pgStore).GetInvoiceStatus()
      internal/store/invoice.go:188
  billing.queue.(*Consumer).process()
      internal/queue/consumer.go:92
Goroutine 447 (running) created at:
  billing.queue.(*Consumer).run()
      internal/queue/consumer.go:61
==================
```

That one is real and it is in our code, but it is a *consequence*, not the cause: the shared mutable thing is the pgx connection pool rows cache, and it only races because two goroutines are touching the same invoice. The race detector found the symptom.

The cause is in the dispatcher, and the detector confirms it independently:

```go test -race -run TestDispatchClosesOverLoopVar ./internal/queue/...
      dispatcher.go:118:36: loop variable id captured by func literal
```

Wait — before I report that as fact, I checked the go.mod. We are on go 1.22, where per-iteration loop variables are the default, so that vet warning is a false positive on this build and the loop variable is *not* the bug. I am calling that out because I nearly filed it. The real reproduction is behavioural, not a race report:

```go run ./cmd/replay --replicas 3 --dates 2026-07-01..2026-07-16
dispatched 41,208 jobs from 3 replicas
distinct invoice ids: 13,736
duplicate pushes: 27,472  (exactly 2 extra per id — every replica pushed every id)
```

Two extra pushes per invoice, not three, because one replica wins the SELECT and the other two overlap it within the same second. That is your one-in-three-hundred: duplicates get deduplicated by the consumer's status check whenever SMTP is fast, and only survive when a redelivery lands inside the SMTP window. Fast SMTP, 0.1 percent of invoices. Slow SMTP at peak, 3 percent. The error rate is a function of mail latency, which is why it looked random to support.

OK so we have both a duplicate-enqueue bug and a check-then-act bug. Which one do we fix, and what is the tradeoff? I am wary of anything that needs a new datastore or a schema migration right now — we have a release freeze until the 24th.

Fix the enqueue bug in full, and fix the check-then-act bug by making it a single atomic statement. Neither needs a migration — that is the part I want to check carefully, because my first instinct was a Postgres advisory lock and that would be the wrong answer.

Enqueue side. The claim has to happen where the rows are selected, not after. One statement, no new table, no advisory locks:

```go
// internal/store/invoice.go
const claimDueInvoices = ```
WITH due AS (
  SELECT id FROM invoices
  WHERE emailed_at IS NULL AND due_at <= now()
  ORDER BY due_at
  LIMIT $1
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
)
UPDATE invoices i
SET claim_token = $2, claimed_at = now()
FROM due
WHERE i.id = due.id
RETURNING i.id
```

FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED is what makes the three replicas cooperate: each one locks and claims a disjoint set of rows, and the other two skip straight past the locked ones instead of blocking. One round trip, no transaction held across the dispatch loop, no new infrastructure. This is the same pattern we already use in the PDF worker at ```internal/queue/pdfWorker.go:142```, so it is not a new idea in this codebase — it is the same idea in a second place.

Tradeoff: SKIP LOCKED means a replica that is slow to claim can leave rows unclaimed for that cycle. With a 30 second dispatch tick that is a 30 second delay on some invoices, which is fine for monthly invoicing and would be completely unacceptable for anything with a seconds-level SLA. Worth stating explicitly so nobody copies this pattern somewhere it does not belong. Second tradeoff: a claimed-but-crashed row stays claimed. I am handling that with a 5 minute claim_token expiry in the WHERE clause, so a dead replica cannot strand invoices permanently.

Consumer side. Replace the read-then-write with a single conditional update, and only send mail if we won:

```go
func (c *Consumer) process(ctx context.Context, job Job) error {
    n, err := c.store.ClaimForEmail(ctx, job.InvoiceID)   // UPDATE ... WHERE emailed_at IS NULL
    if err != nil { return err }
    if n == 0 { return nil }                              // someone else already emailed it
    if err := c.mailer.Send(ctx, job); err != nil {
        c.store.ReleaseEmailClaim(ctx, job.InvoiceID)     // put it back, do not strand it
        return err
    }
    return c.store.MarkEmailed(ctx, job.InvoiceID)
}
```

Both are single UPDATE statements against the existing emailed_at column, so no migration. The behaviour change is that "claimed but not yet emailed" is now a real state, which means SMTP failure needs an explicit release path — I added ReleaseEmailClaim for exactly that, and without it a transient SMTP outage would silently stop invoicing for those customers rather than producing an error.

The honest residual: this makes duplicate *emails* impossible for a given invoice id, but it does not make duplicate *enqueue* invisible. We will still push 3x the jobs we need unless the claim query lands. Both need to ship together; the consumer change alone reduces customer-visible damage, the claim change removes the waste.
Both go in. Now — shutdown. Last time we deployed I watched the queue get cut off mid-send and I am not doing that again during a freeze. What happens to in-flight jobs when a pod gets SIGTERM?

Right now: they die. consumer.go has no signal handling at all. Kubernetes sends SIGTERM, the process exits, and anything between the ClaimForEmail and the MarkEmailed is gone — claimed, never emailed, and with the 5 minute claim expiry that is a 5 minute delay per stranded invoice, in a rolling deploy with three replicas that is a continuous trickle of late invoices for the whole rollout.

Three-stage drain, and the ordering matters:

```go
func (c *Consumer) Shutdown(ctx context.Context) error {
    c.draining.Store(true)                    // 1. stop claiming new work
    c.queue.Stop()                             // 2. no more dispatches into this pod
    done := make(chan struct{})
    go func() { c.wg.Wait(); close(done) }()   // 3. wait for in-flight handlers
    select {
    case <-done:
        return nil
    case <-ctx.Done():
        // Hard stop. Anything still in flight is re-queued by claim_token expiry.
        c.log.Warn("drain timed out, in-flight jobs will be reclaimed after claim expiry",
            zap.Int("in_flight", c.inFlight.Load()))
        return ctx.Err()
    }
}
```

The important part is the third stage and the timeout. Waiting for wg with no bound is a worse failure mode than exiting: an SMTP call that hangs for 120 seconds holds the pod in Terminating, the deployment stalls, and after the 300 second grace period Kubernetes SIGKILLs you anyway — so you get a hard kill with none of the logging. A 25 second drain budget against a 30 second grace period leaves room for the process to exit cleanly and actually log what it abandoned.

There is a subtlety with the release path. If a send is genuinely in flight when we time out, we cannot safely call ReleaseEmailClaim — the SMTP call might still succeed, and we would re-send. Letting the claim_token expire is the correct behaviour there: worst case one invoice is delayed by the 5 minute expiry, and no customer ever gets two emails. I would rather delay than duplicate; that asymmetry is the whole point.

I am also adding a readiness probe change. Today readiness is a bare liveness-style check, so Kubernetes keeps routing traffic to a pod that is draining and has stopped claiming, and the dispatcher happily pushes work that sits unclaimed until expiry. Readiness needs to flip false the moment draining is set, so the rolling deploy shifts load before we stop taking it. That one-line change is what makes the rest of the sequence work; without it the drain logic is correct and unreachable.
Good. Make sure this is idempotent though — if the claim or the release fails halfway, I do not want an invoice that can never be emailed again. And I want to know when it happens.

Both are reasonable and they interact, so let me walk the failure matrix rather than assert that it is fine.

The dangerous state is claimed-but-never-emailed with no path out. There are three ways to get there: the process dies between ClaimForEmail and Send, Send succeeds and MarkEmailed fails, or ReleaseEmailClaim itself fails. The claim_token expiry covers the first two only if the expiry query actually re-selects claimed rows — so here is the query, and this is the part that is easy to get wrong:

```go
const claimForEmail = ```
UPDATE invoices
SET claim_token = $1, claimed_at = now(), email_attempts = email_attempts + 1
WHERE id = $2
  AND emailed_at IS NULL
  AND (claim_token IS NULL OR claimed_at < now() - interval '5 minutes')
RETURNING id
```

Without the claimed_at clause this returns zero rows forever after the first claim, and that invoice is permanently unemailed. The expiry window is 5 minutes, which is 10x our p99 SMTP latency of roughly 30 seconds — wide enough that a slow but healthy send is never stolen out from under a live worker.

A permanent block would need claim_token to be set, claimed_at to be fresh, and email_attempts to keep growing forever, which cannot happen: every attempt either emails, releases, or ages out. I am satisfied that the state machine terminates. What I will not claim is that it terminates fast in every case — the worst realistic outcome is one invoice delayed by up to 5 minutes, forever, if the mailer is down and every attempt hits the SMTP timeout. That is an alerting problem, not a correctness problem, and it is why the metric below is a page and not a dashboard tile.

For observability, four signals:

```go
billing_queue_email_claims_total{result="won"}         // increment on the n==1 path
billing_queue_email_claims_total{result="lost"}        // increment on the n==0 path
billing_queue_email_stranded_total                     // email_attempts >= 3 with emailed_at still NULL
billing_queue_drain_inflight                           // gauge, sampled every second during drain
```

The "lost" counter is the interesting one. It is not an error — it is the duplicate suppression working, and after this change it should equal the duplicate push count we measured at 27,472 for the replay window. If it is near zero, the claim query is not actually preventing duplicate enqueues and something regressed. If it is far above the duplicate push count, workers are racing on claims we did not expect and I would want to see the dispatch side.

The stranded counter gets a page at 1 for five minutes, not a dashboard tile, because one stranded invoice is a customer who never got their invoice and support will find out before we do. Page on 1, deliberately. I would rather be wrong once than be quiet for a month.

I am also bumping email_attempts in the same UPDATE rather than in a separate statement, so a crash between claim and send still records that an attempt happened. If it were a separate write we would lose the count exactly in the case we most want it — the crash case — and the stranded metric would under-report during the incident it exists to catch.
Ship it and give me the numbers.

Shipped as billing-ingest v2.8.0. The diff:

```
 internal/store/invoice.go         | 96 +++++++--  claimDueInvoices, claimForEmail, releaseEmailClaim
 internal/queue/dispatcher.go      | 41 ++--     single claim query, no per-goroutine push
 internal/queue/consumer.go        | 73 ++++--    claim-then-send, drain, signal handling
 internal/queue/pdfWorker.go       |   0          (read as reference only, unchanged)
 internal/queue/consumer_test.go   | 214 +++++    11 new tests
 cmd/replay/main.go                | 18 +         --replicas flag for the repro
 5 files changed, 402 insertions(+), 61 deletions(-)
```

No migration, as promised. Tests: 11 new, covering concurrent claim (50 goroutines racing for the same invoice, exactly one wins), claim expiry reclaim, release-then-reclaim, drain-under-load, drain timeout with in-flight work, and the "send succeeded but MarkEmailed failed" recovery path. Full package green under ```go test -race -count=50 ./internal/queue/...``` — 6 minutes, no race reports, which is the first clean run that command has ever produced on this package.

Numbers, from the same ```replay``` harness over 2026-07-01..07-16 that previously produced 27,472 duplicate pushes:

- Duplicate pushes: 27,472 to 0. The claim query hands each invoice to exactly one replica.
- Dispatched jobs: 41,208 to 13,736 — a 3x reduction in queue volume, which is the throughput win nobody asked for but everyone gets.
- Duplicate emails in the replay: 0. Previously one in three hundred.
- p99 dispatch latency: 240ms to 310ms, the expected cost of the UPDATE ... RETURNING round trip.
- Reclaims from claim expiry over the 16 day window: 61, all of them SMTP timeouts, all eventually emailed. Zero stranded at email_attempts >= 3.

Known gaps, stated plainly. The 5 minute claim expiry means a genuinely dead mailer delays invoices by up to 5 minutes each, and the stranded page fires at 1, so during a mailer outage we will page and that is intended. And the claim query is Postgres-specific — the FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED syntax will not survive the MySQL migration that has been on the roadmap for two quarters, so whoever does that will need to translate it, and this is the one place in the queue that cannot be expressed portably. I would rather it be a known sharp edge than hidden behind a repository abstraction that quietly does not lock on MySQL.
